transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-06-19
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Lena Ortiz (Redwood SE), Chris Wu (Redwood), Maya Chen (CTO - CypressAI), Diego Ramos (Infra), Priya Nair (ML Eng), Tom Bell (Product)

Summary (auto): CypressAI is migrating from a mixed hosted/proto stack and wants dedicated reserved capacity for production. They have strict isolation requirements for PII-adjacent workloads and tight 99th percentile latency goals for interactive features. Discussed warm pools, prewarming, burst mechanics, and encryption.

[00:00] Samir: Hey everyone, thanks for making time. We wanted to kick off by understanding your current infra and what you're trying to protect with isolation, cause that will drive the dedicated config. Maya, do you want to start?
[00:10] Maya: Yeah, sure. Uh, thanks. So we, we've been running a mix of hosted APIs for early traffic and some self-hosted nodes for internal tooling. Our plan is to flip customer-facing interactive features to a dedicated pool, because, uh, the compliance team wants tenant isolation and auditability.
[00:25] Diego: And to add, we need burst capacity for marketing spikes around new feature releases. Typically a 3x QPS spike for a few hours, maybe up to six. And prewarm times are a thing — cold-starts kill the SLO.
[00:36] Lena: Totally. That's where Reserved + warm pools/ hotpools come in. We can reserve GPU nodes and configure warm pools so the KV cache and model weights stay resident. Question for you — are you comfortable with multi-tenant on node-level fencing, or do you want strict single-tenant nodes?
[00:50] Priya: For PII-adjacent requests we need logical isolation; ideally dedicated nodes per-tenant for those enterprise customers. For the rest, shared warm pool is fine as long as we can pin model versions and audit token usage per customer.
[01:05] Tom: Also, about encryption — we need KMS/HSM integration, and our security team wants proof of key custody separation for logs.
[01:12] Chris: We do support both bring-your-own-kms and managed KMS. We can show the KMS flow in the architecture doc.

[01:25] Maya: Can you explain the fallback behavior if the reserved pool is saturated during a big spike? We cannot afford request drops.
[01:32] Samir: Yeah, good question. We typically set routing policies: tiered fallback to compatible hosted variants, or cross-region fallback if you have dedicated capacity in more than one region. There's also the option to define burst tiers — pre-approved burst capacity that kicks in automatically but billed separately.
[01:47] Diego: Is the fallback synchronous? Like, if we route to hosted, do we lose the KV cache and get higher latencies?
[01:53] Lena: Correct, you'll typically go to a variant that may not have the same KV cache warm state, so cold cache latency will be higher. But for many workloads that only need short single-turn responses it's acceptable. For conversational agents that rely on context windows, we recommend keeping a warm pool large enough to handle peak QPS.

[02:10] Priya: What's the unit economics here? We're looking at ML-heavy workloads — long contexts, 8k tokens typical, and a lot of sampling.
[02:18] Samir: For long contexts the cost per token increases but reserved nodes lower the per-token bill compared to on-demand hosted. We can model costs based on your perf profile once you send sample prompts and expected QPS.

[02:30] Diego: We run on GCP for most infra. How does network topology look for VPC connectivity? We can't open public endpoints for certain customers.
[02:38] Lena: For Private deployments we can offer a customer-managed control plane with VPC peering or private link. There's also an on-prem option if you need air-gapped. The dedicated offering supports VPC-only endpoints with SAML SSO and RBAC mapping.
[02:52] Maya: And audit logs? We need immutable logs for each request for audits.
[02:57] Chris: We stream request metadata to your SIEM over secure channels; logs include model version, tokens consumed, request traces, and user identifiers if provided. Logs can be configured to avoid raw PII if you prefer.

[03:10] Tom: Practically, what does prewarming look like? We hate paying for always-on nodes, but cold starts are rough.
[03:17] Lena: Two patterns: warm pool (idle-but-ready nodes) and predictive prewarm where we bring up capacity ahead of expected spikes. Warm pools maintain model weights and KV cache for pinned models. The warm-pool size is a lever: smaller pools save cost but increase chance of cold starts during spikes.
[03:33] Diego: Hmm, if our spikes are 3x for 2-6 hours, what's your recommendation for pool sizing?
[03:39] Lena: We usually recommend sizing the warm pool to handle baseline plus 60-80% of an expected spike, and then allow burst to stretch to 100% with pre-approval. For your scenario we might recommend reserving an 8-GPU pool and configure a hotpool of 2-4 extra GPUs for immediate burst while autoscaling brings up additional nodes.
[03:57] Priya: Are GPUs preemptible? We need stable performance for deterministic latency.
[04:03] Samir: Dedicated reserved nodes are non-preemptible. The burst nodes can be configured as dedicated reserved or on-demand depending on your budget and risk tolerance.

[04:15] Maya: What about model variants and quantization? We need to support a larger full-precision model for higher-quality generation for premium customers and a quantized cheaper variant for others. How does Redwood handle routing and consistent outputs?
[04:28] Lena: You can declare model variants and map them to routing policies (by customer tier). We surface a model catalog and let you pin versions per tenant. Output differences are possible; we recommend eval sets to monitor quality regression when switching variants. Redwood Optimize can suggest quantization profiles and run eval checks on rollouts.

[04:50] Diego: We also have concerns about burst billing surprises. Can you do rate shapers or per-route quotas so we don't accidentally blow budget during a campaign?
[04:58] Chris: Yes, we support per-route quotas, token caps, and rate limiting. You can set hard caps and soft caps with alerts. Billing for burst can be pre-bound — you can pre-approve x hours of burst per month and any overage gets escalated.

[05:12] Priya: On benchmarks — what do you need from us to run an accurate bench? We want to see 99p latency and token throughput numbers.
[05:19] Samir: Send a representative prompt set (ideally 1000 queries with distribution), expected QPS profile, and your target 99p latency SLO. We'll run a 2-hour bench on a reserved staging pool and share token/hour, 99p latency, and cost estimates.
[05:35] Tom: If we go Private on-prem, how long is integration and what's the support model?
[05:40] Lena: On-prem installs typically take 6-12 weeks depending on network complexity and compliance packaging. Private (VPC) deployments are faster. Support tiers can include on-call SEs and operational runbooks. For regulated customers we also offer extended audit/forensics support.

[05:55] Maya: Any gotchas for logging/PII? We need to ensure logs do not contain raw PII for certain customers.
[06:00] Chris: You can toggle PII redaction at the ingress layer and ensure logs only contain hashed identifiers. We can also route raw payloads to your S3 with customer side encryption if needed.

[06:12] Diego: Let's talk scaling expectations. Right now peak baseline is 120 QPS with 8k token contexts and maybe 20-30k tokens/sec at peak. We expect 2x growth by Q4. Want to be able to plan for a 2-3x growth scenario without re-architecting.
[06:27] Samir: We can map that to a growth plan: start with an 8-GPU reserved pool, add automated scaling policies, and plan a snapshot of performance monthly. We'll provide threshold alerts and a quarterly architecture sync.

[06:40] Priya: Any limitations around model size? We want to eventually serve 70B models with long contexts.
[06:45] Lena: Our runtime supports models up to certain memory footprints depending on GPU type; for 70B we recommend multi-GPU sharded serving and we'll need to validate with a sample model. There are options: ZeRO-style sharding, kv-cache distribution, and we can optimize kernels for longer context.

[06:58] Maya: For the pilot, are we constrained to a single region? We have users in EMEA and NA.
[07:03] Samir: Pilot can be multi-region. For production, cross-region failover is supported. Keep in mind data residency and latency — pin tidbits by region if required.

[07:12] Diego: Who else at Redwood should we expect to be involved in the bench?
[07:15] Samir: SEs (Lena), Performance Eng, and Solutions (Chris) will run the bench. We'll also loop in our security engineer if you want the SOC2/package review.

[07:25] Tom: Any SLA numbers at the reserved level?
[07:28] Chris: Reserved Dedicated comes with SLA guarantees around availability and latency targets, depends on contract tier. We'll include SLA language in the pricing packet.

[07:35] Priya: Do you have anonymized examples of warm-pool sizing for a similar SaaS app?
[07:39] Lena: Yes, we can share anonymized case studies showing warm-pool:baseline ratios and cost delta. I'll attach those in the follow-up.

[07:47] Maya: Ok let's get concrete — what would a minimal pilot look like?
[07:51] Samir: Minimal pilot: 2-week reserved pool (8 GPUs) with warm-pool config, a 2-hour benchmark run during the pilot, and an intake of your prompt set. We'll instrument token level cost and 99p latency and provide recommendations for burst sizing.

[08:05] Diego: Sounds good. One last question: if we need tenant-level single-node isolation for top customers, can we add nodes later without downtime?
[08:12] Lena: Yes, we support live node reallocation and can bring up isolated nodes and migrate tenants with connection draining. There might be short warm times for warmed caches, but the routing will avoid traffic during migration windows.

Recap & Next steps:
[08:30] Samir: Recap — we'll send pricing for 8-GPU reserved + burst options, Lena will share dedicated architecture and prewarm docs, CypressAI will provide sample prompts and QPS profile, and we'll schedule a 2-hour bench next week (proposal: 2026-06-25).

[08:45] Maya: Looks good. We'll aim to upload materials by Tuesday.
[08:50] Priya: I'll get the prompt set and a small traffic trace.
[08:53] Samir: Great, thanks everyone. We'll follow up with calendar invites and the SOW draft.

End of transcript.

Notes: occasional transcriber mislabels — e.g., "K V cache" instead of "KV cache"; some acronyms spelled out (S O C 2). There's slight overlap and crosstalk around 04:00-04:20 when pricing vs prewarming was discussed.
